newsitem.title: UK: Kinnock vows to get tough on EU air travel market.
newsitem.headline: Kinnock vows to get tough on EU air travel market.

text.p: Full liberalisation of the European Union's aviation market, which is due to be completed next year, will require rigorous enforcement of EU competition laws, Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said on Monday.

In a speech due to be made later today to an industry conference in London, Kinnock said that the Commission is "going to have to give more focused attention to potential abuse of market power by dominant carriers in specific national and regional markets within the EU".

Air fares within the EU market were generally still too high but he told the SBC Warburg European Transport Conference that it would take time for new competition to break through the structural barriers of congested airports and markets dominated by the former flag carriers.

"Against this background I think you will understand why I feel that rigorous enforcement of the EU's competition rules, as well as of its state aid rules, is going to be essential to the ultimate success of the liberalisation process," he said.
He said the Commission would have to: "Examine mergers, joint ventures or alliances which appear to have the effect of restricting competition.
"Assess possible anti-competitive use of facilities such as slots and computer reservation systems...(and) respond to complaints of predatory practices that arise."
He also warned he might "have to consider the possibility" of the Commission examining high fare levels on specific routes.
From April next year European airlines will have the right to compete on all domestic as well as international routes within the Union, regardless of nationality.

But Kinnock said he expected EU member nations would also adopt a new directive "within a few weeks" at the Transport Council to open up the market for ground handling services to full competition at most major EU airports by 1999.

He said he was also now looking at airport landing and passenger handling charges which he said varied considerably across the EU, "and there is as yet no comparable basis of calculation from one airport to another".
"I have consequently issued a consultation document on the subject and I will be seeking to produce relevant proposals when that process is complete."

Finally the Commission was to make a proposal for revising EU rules on how airports allocate their takeoff and landing slots later this year, in an attempt to give new competition a better chance of gaining entry to the more congested airports.
Kinnock said one idea being considered was to create a market for airlines to trade their slots.

"Establishing a market for slots is also an appealing idea since it reflects the commercial value of the capacity, provided, of course, that there are adequate safeguards for newcomers to withstand the pressure of dominant carriers with substantial resources."
